{"answer":"Nigeria’s Constitution divides responsibilities among **federal, state and local government**:

- **Federal government:** The National Assembly makes laws on matters reserved for the federation. Examples include defence, currency, citizenship and aviation. [e0fdcfd0-bd2e-43f6-904b-2fc73d07507f, 8e886cbe-bcfe-4e76-9f95-c2a94df7213f]
- **State governments:** A State House of Assembly makes laws for its state on matters outside the federal-only list, and on shared matters to the extent the Constitution allows. States also make laws setting out the structure, finances and functions of local government councils. [50cf38f8-c1ad-4abb-a112-7994f61546b6, 40b1819c-48ca-4478-bfa6-da580d1aa205]
- **Local government councils:** Their listed functions include markets and motor parks, local roads and drains, refuse disposal, and registering births, deaths and marriages. They also participate with the state in primary education, agriculture and health services. [278fb615-3343-4a6b-9dc3-b1844f448c1d, f8387941-e0e0-4011-8299-1bfec8077733]","citation_ids":["e0fdcfd0-bd2e-43f6-904b-2fc73d07507f","8e886cbe-bcfe-4e76-9f95-c2a94df7213f","50cf38f8-c1ad-4abb-a112-7994f61546b6","40b1819c-48ca-4478-bfa6-da580d1aa205","278fb615-3343-4a6b-9dc3-b1844f448c1d","f8387941-e0e0-4011-8299-1bfec8077733"]}

{
  "answer": "Chapter IV of the Nigerian Constitution sets out these fundamental rights:\n\n- **Life, dignity and personal liberty.** Dignity includes protection against torture, slavery and forced labour, subject to the qualifications stated in the Constitution. [fc4e2cbe-dc0e-42e7-a8de-540d4cd639ac, cf89f75d-fa5a-4b13-a607-c2d1950efc44, c8c4bacb-daaf-4588-8b03-b43387004b17]\n- **A fair hearing** in the determination of your civil rights or a criminal charge. [5dac4c54-e6c8-4ebe-894c-bc785787755f]\n- **Privacy** of your home and communications; **freedom of thought, conscience and religion**; and **freedom of expression**. [e5bdbaef-a982-4cef-aa9a-a5e00e05d376, 79599790-5d4f-4ddc-87fa-393c30f556d1, 70eaa7ec-23cc-4a26-9106-34ab692a377b]\n- **Peaceful assembly and association**, including joining a trade union or other association. [edec7a6a-1b71-490d-8a31-64e67d95749e]\n- **Freedom of movement and residence in Nigeria**, for Nigerian citizens. [b5b43f29-8543-4695-aa09-bfdfb936dd9b]\n- **Freedom from specified forms of discrimination** against Nigerian citizens, including discrimination based on ethnic group, place of origin, sex, religion, political opinion or circumstances of birth. [6ddf3333-a1fa-4751-ac36-c1cc6952c89f]\n\nChapter IV also lists the right to acquire and own immovable property anywhere in Nigeria and provisions on compulsory acquisition of property. The retrieved passage lists these headings but does not provide the detailed rules. [96f2fb0e-0694-4d4e-b4f0-13b2bca04db3]\n\n**These rights have qualifications.** For example, the Constitution permits certain laws restricting privacy, religion, expression, assembly and movement where they are reasonably justifiable in a democratic society for specified purposes. [fb5bb748-aca4-4e41-ba4d-719d2524e20b]",

answer: {"answer":"The passages I found do not directly say whether police may arrest you **without a warrant**, so I cannot give a definite yes or no from this library. The Constitution says a person may be deprived of liberty only in cases and through procedures permitted by law, including on reasonable suspicion of a criminal offence. That does not, by itself, establish when a police officer can dispense with a warrant. [c8c4bacb-daaf-4588-8b03-b43387004b17, 285b9811-a816-4894-a462-41d1b9732712]\n\nIf you are arrested, the Constitution says you may remain silent until you have consulted a lawyer or another person of your choice. It also says you must be told the grounds for your arrest in writing, in a language you understand, within 24 hours. [c8c4bacb-daaf-4588-8b03-b43387004b17, 339879f8-c29f-48cb-bcc5-f00aad24bc9a]","citation_ids":["c8c4bacb-daaf-4588-8b03-b43387004b17","285b9811-a816-4894-a462-41d1b9732712","339879f8-c29f-48cb-bcc5-f00aad24bc9a"]}
